title: Minimally Counterintuitive Concepts
description: Religion as a by-product of ordinary minds, Boyer's templates and the Mickey Mouse problem

concepts.title: Religion as a By-product of Ordinary Minds
concepts.contentHtml:
An earlier course met the cognitive science of religion (CSR) in outline. Here you take its claims apart, starting with the founding one: the naturalness of religion thesis. In 2000 Justin Barrett described a new cognitive approach suggesting that seemingly extraordinary religious thoughts and behaviours can be supported by quite ordinary cognition.1 A decade later he put it more bluntly. Ordinary minds in ordinary environments typically arrive at some belief in supernatural agency, so special cultural scaffolding is unnecessary: supernaturalism falls near a natural anchor point.2

The view is often called the standard model. Religion is an evolutionary by-product, a side effect of capacities that evolved for other jobs, not an adaptation in its own right. There is no religion module. Instead, as the anthropologist Pascal Boyer argued in 2003, religious concepts activate several functionally distinct mental systems that also work in non-religious contexts, and they tweak the usual inferences of those systems.3 His list covers the detection of animacy and agency, social exchange, moral intuitions, precaution against natural hazards and the understanding of misfortune.

Two qualifications keep the thesis honest. First, natural means early and effortless, not inevitable. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (SEP) notes that treating most people as implicit believers, for whom religious thinking is the path of least resistance, does not strictly imply that religion is innate. Second, the intuitive layer can diverge from official doctrine. Believers often show theologically incorrect ideas in fast, online thinking that they explicitly reject on reflection, and even atheists who deny that ghosts exist occasionally show fear responses to them in the lab.

By-product theorists disagree about which mental tools matter most. This lesson takes the first candidate, Boyer's account of why some supernatural ideas are catchier than others. Later lessons test agency detection, mind-reading, ritual and the rival claim that religion is an adaptation.

concepts.title: Boyer's Templates and the Memory Advantage
concepts.contentHtml:
Boyer's theory starts from intuitive ontology: the categories people apply spontaneously, distinguishing persons, animals, plants, artefacts and natural objects, each carrying default expectations from folk physics, folk biology and folk psychology.1 A minimally counterintuitive (MCI) concept violates one or two of those expectations and leaves the rest intact. Violations come in two kinds. A breach removes an expectation: an invisible mountain breaches physicality. A transfer imports one from another category: a statue that grows has borrowed biology. Barrett later turned this into a coding scheme so that researchers could count violations and quantify counterintuitiveness.

Why should such concepts spread? Because they grab attention while staying easy to reason with. A ghost is a person who walks through walls, but everything else you know about persons (wants, beliefs, grudges) still applies, so the idea is rich in inferences. A concept that breaks everything is hard to remember and hard to use.

The early experiments looked promising. In four experiments published in 2001, Barrett and Melanie Nyhof found that 48 American students recalled expectation-violating items from unfamiliar folk stories better than mundane ones.2 In chains of retelling, such items were passed on more successfully than common items or merely bizarre ones (unusual, but consistent with their category), and the advantage persisted after three months. In 2006 Ara Norenzayan, Scott Atran and colleagues found that a story template of mostly intuitive concepts with a minority of counterintuitive ones was remembered best after a week. Among the Grimm Brothers' tales, those that became culturally successful were especially likely to fit that template.3

Later work was less tidy. A 2016 critical review by Benjamin Purzycki and Aiyana Willard is one of several challenges to MCI theory, and Willard, Joseph Henrich and Norenzayan argued the same year that memory effects decrease as MCI concepts become commonly used. Keep the theory's scope in view: it explains why ideas are memorable, not why anyone believes them.

concepts.title: The Mickey Mouse and Zeus Problems
concepts.contentHtml:
If minimal counterintuitiveness made gods, Mickey Mouse would have temples. A talking mouse violates the folk-psychological expectation that animals cannot use language, just as neatly as a spirit violates folk physics, yet nobody prays to him. Scott Atran pressed the point in In Gods We Trust (2002), and it became the Mickey Mouse problem: cognitive theories struggle to predict which MCI agents are believed in and worshipped.

In 2010 Will Gervais and Joseph Henrich sharpened it into the Zeus problem. Zeus has every content feature that supposedly makes gods successful and was once the target of widespread belief and worship. He no longer is, so content alone cannot explain belief.1 Their answer was context biases: learners adopt beliefs depending on who holds them and how. The most discussed is the bias toward credibility-enhancing displays (CREDs), Henrich's 2009 proposal that people preferentially trust claims backed by costly or hard-to-fake behaviour such as ritual participation, taboo observance or celibacy.2 Experiments support part of this. Willard, Henrich and Norenzayan found that MCI content was less believable than intuitive content, but that watching a CRED increased belief in it.3

Others think content still matters. In 2019 Thomas Swan and Jamin Halberstadt asked participants to invent either a religious or a fictional agent with five supernatural abilities. Invented gods received more abilities that violated folk psychology, such as reading minds, or that were ambiguous, violating several domains at once. They were also rated more beneficial and more ambivalent, mixing potential benefit and harm. Mickey, on this view, lacks the beneficence, ambivalence and ambiguity that a god needs.4

The two answers need not compete. Content may decide which ideas are catchy and which could be worshipped; context may decide which of those your own community actually believes. That division of labour, with cognition supplying candidates and culture choosing among them, recurs through the rest of this course.

title: Agency Detection, Mind-Reading and Purpose
description: HADD and its tests, theory of mind and the autism debate, and children's promiscuous teleology

concepts.title: Faces in the Clouds: the Agency Detector
concepts.contentHtml:
Stewart Guthrie's Faces in the Clouds (1993) argued that we are naturally inclined to see the world in terms of agency: faces in clouds, in trees, in almost anything. Darwin had noticed a rudimentary version in his dog, which barked at movement without any apparent cause, as if a mysterious agent were present.1 Building on both, Justin Barrett argued in 2000 that the propensity extends to intentional agents in general, anything with self-propelled, purposeful, goal-directed behaviour. His 2004 book Why Would Anyone Believe in God? helped popularise the name hypersensitive agency detection device, or HADD.

The logic is error management. Picture a branch snapping in a dark forest. Mistaking the wind for a predator costs a moment's fright; mistaking a predator for the wind can cost your life. A detector tuned to those lopsided costs should produce many false alarms, and false alarms are what spirits might grow from. David Maij and colleagues point out that the reasoning has the same structure as Pascal's Wager.2

It is an elegant story, and the evidence for it is thin. In 2013 Michiel van Elk asked believers and sceptics to spot a human figure in point-light displays. Paranormal believers more often reported an agent when none was present, but illusory agency detection was unrelated to traditional religious belief.3 Maij, Hein van Schie and van Elk then ran six threat-inducing experiments with 233 participants. Threats that were weak (threatening pictures, classical horror music) or moderate (virtual reality) did not increase false detection of agents or intentions.4 Participants generally leaned towards assuming agents were absent, and detection was unrelated to supernatural belief.

The authors suggested future work focus on expectations: someone raised on horror films may expect dangerous agents in a dark forest. Defenders of HADD have answered critics with modifications rather than retreat, so the debate is open. Either way, as Michael Murray noted, HADD is unlikely to give a complete account of religious belief.

concepts.title: Mind-Reading and the Autism Debate
concepts.contentHtml:
Detecting an agent is only the start; next you want to know what it is thinking. Theory of mind, or mentalising, is the capacity to attribute beliefs, desires and intentions to others. Gods in most traditions are minds that know, want, judge and respond, so belief may lean on mentalising. It is also hard to stop reading the mind of someone you loved after they die, which may encourage thoughts of an afterlife.

If belief leans on mentalising, people who mentalise less should believe less. In 2012 Ara Norenzayan, Will Gervais and Kali Trzesniewski tested this. Their first study was small: 12 autistic and 13 matched neurotypical adolescents from the same South Florida neighbourhood. The autistic participants were only 11% as likely to strongly endorse God.1 In a Canadian student sample and two American national samples, the autism spectrum predicted weaker belief in God, and mentalising, measured with the Empathy Quotient, statistically mediated the link. Mentalising also appeared to explain the long-known gender gap in which men report less religious belief than women.

The finding drew wide attention, and then a much larger test. In 2017 Maij, van Elk, Gervais and colleagues ran five studies with over 67,000 participants in the Netherlands, Switzerland and the United States. The Empathy Quotient and the Autism-Spectrum Quotient did not predict belief in supernatural agents in any of the three countries, though there was a curvilinear effect in the United States.2 What did predict belief, strongly, was exposure to credibility-enhancing displays: how much people had seen others act out their faith during their upbringing.

Notice that Gervais is an author on both papers, a sign of a field willing to correct itself. The SEP now lists the autism claim among the contested ideas of CSR. Mentalising may make gods thinkable, but the large studies point to cultural learning as the stronger influence on who actually believes.

concepts.title: Born Believers? Purpose, Dualism and the Afterlife
concepts.contentHtml:
Deborah Kelemen found that young children favour teleological, purpose-based explanations of nature, a broad bias later called promiscuous teleology: rocks are pointy so that animals can scratch themselves. In a 2004 review she asked whether children are “intuitive theists”, disposed to see natural things as the product of non-human design, and suggested the label may fit by around the age of five.

The bias does not vanish with schooling; it hides. In 2009 Kelemen and Rosset had undergraduates judge explanations under time pressure. Speeded participants accepted more scientifically unwarranted teleological claims, such as “the sun radiates heat because warmth nurtures life”, without making more errors on control items.1 In 2013 Kelemen and colleagues tested physical scientists from top-ranked American universities. Under speed, the scientists also accepted more unwarranted teleology. Their overall endorsement was lower than that of undergraduates and community members, yet no lower than that of humanities scholars.2

A second intuition is dualism: from early in life we seem to treat minds and bodies as very different things, which fits ethnographic reports of spirit possession. Jesse Bering and David Bjorklund interviewed children and adults about a dead agent. Even 4- to 6-year-olds said that biological processes stop at death, yet older children and adults still attributed knowledge, emotions and desires to the dead.3 Bering's related idea, existential theory of mind, holds that births, deaths, diseases and tragedies are often implicitly read as happening for a reason.

In Why Religion Is Natural and Science Is Not (2011), Robert McCauley calls such thinking maturationally natural: it arrives early and without instruction, unlike science and, interestingly, unlike theology, which must be laboriously learned. Note what this does not show. Natural is neither true nor false, and the next lessons show that culture still decides which gods, if any, a child ends up believing in.

title: Ritual, Costly Signals and Commitment
description: Commune survival, fire-walking hearts, painful festivals and Whitehouse's two modes of religiosity

concepts.title: Costly Signals: Why Strict Communes Last
concepts.contentHtml:
The by-product view explains why religious ideas are easy to think. A rival tradition asks what religion does. Its puzzle is cost: rituals, taboos and sacrifices consume time, wealth and sometimes blood. The costly signalling theory of religion answers that costly practices work as hard-to-fake badges of commitment. Anyone can claim loyalty, but only the committed will fast, keep dawn prayers or submit to painful rites, so groups that demand such displays can screen out free-riders and trust one another more.

The best-known test used history as a laboratory. Richard Sosis and Eric Bressler collected data on the constraints and ritual requirements that 83 nineteenth-century American communes imposed on their members. Every commune faces the same collective-action problem: cooperate in the fields or collapse. Religious communes, with an average life of just over 25 years, lasted more than three times longer than secular ones, and secular communes were about three times more likely to dissolve in any given year.1 The results supported aspects of costly signalling theory, and the authors were candid about the theory's shortcomings.

Field experiments followed. In studies of Israeli kibbutzim by Sosis and Ruffle, signals appropriate to each community (synagogue attendance in religious kibbutzim, communal dining in secular ones) were correlated with cooperation in an economic game. The commitment logic, in other words, is not unique to religion; religion may simply supply unusually costly and visible signals.

Signalling is not the only way to read costly acts. Henrich's CRED theory from lesson 1 says such displays persuade learners that a belief is sincerely held, rather than proving loyalty to peers. A 2022 analysis by Brusse, Handfield and Zollman concluded that the two models have deep structural differences and cannot be reduced to one another. As a result, they can be seen as complementary rather than in competition,2 and the authors set out the differing predictions that future studies could use to tell them apart.

concepts.title: Extreme Rituals in the Field
concepts.contentHtml:
Every year at midnight on 23 June, in San Pedro Manrique, a Spanish village of 600 people, fire-walkers cross a bed of embers in an amphitheatre that holds up to 3,000 spectators. The fire consumes more than two tons of oak wood and burns for four hours. Most walkers carry another person on their back, typically a spouse, relative or friend, and on arrival are hugged by those closest to them. In the ritual studied by Ivana Konvalinka, Dimitris Xygalatas and colleagues, 28 people crossed coals 7 metres long with surface temperatures of 677 °C.1

The team recorded heart rates from 12 fire-walkers and 26 spectators. Using recurrence analysis, a method for comparing the dynamics of time series, they found fine-grained commonalities of arousal between walkers and the spectators who were their friends or relatives, but not visiting strangers.2 The related spectators' bodies were doing something very different from the walkers', so the shared arousal was not imitation of movement. The authors suggest the link may be informational, carried by what the event meant to each watcher.

Does such intensity make people more generous? In a 2013 study during the Hindu festival of Thaipusam in Mauritius, Xygalatas and colleagues compared two ritual practices, one a painful high-ordeal rite. Of the 86 men studied, 19 actively performed the ordeal.3 Both performing it and merely observing it were associated with greater social cohesion and cooperative behaviour, measured economically as higher generosity.

These are field studies with modest samples rather than randomised experiments, and they cannot rule out every alternative explanation. They show that intense ritual can do real social work, binding performers to those who care about them. They do not by themselves show that this work is why such rituals exist, which is the question the adaptationist needs answered.

concepts.title: Two Modes of Religiosity and Identity Fusion
concepts.contentHtml:
The anthropologist Harvey Whitehouse proposes that rituals settle into two shapes because of how memory works. In the doctrinal mode, rituals are frequently repeated. Frequent repetition activates semantic memory for religious teachings, general knowledge you can rarely date, and implicit memory for ritual procedure.1 That favours anonymous communities, religious leaders, orthodoxy checks and centralisation, so the religion can spread widely.

In the imagistic mode, rituals are rare and, without exception, highly arousing: traumatic initiations, ecstatic cult practices, collective possession. Rarely performed and highly arousing rituals trigger vivid and enduring episodic memories, sometimes so vivid that psychologists call them flashbulb memories.2 The result is intense cohesion within small, localised, exclusive groups whose ideas are hard to spread. The two modes often occur together within a single tradition and interact.

Whitehouse's later work centres on identity fusion, a visceral feeling of oneness in which personal and group identities fuse, associated with extreme pro-group commitment ranging from charity to willingness to die for the group. His shared-experiences pathway says that undergoing powerful, often dysphoric experiences together produces fusion. Evidence has come from Bostonians after the 2013 marathon bombings and from Libyan insurgents in the 2011 conflict. In a preregistered survey of 1,632 Britons published in 2024, those who reported more intense sadness during Queen Elizabeth II's funeral showed higher fusion and pledged more to a monarchist charity.3

Compare this with costly signalling. Signalling is about information passing between people who need to trust one another; fusion is about what a shared ordeal does to each participant's sense of self. Different rituals may run on different mechanisms, and lesson 6 shows the modes theory reappearing in the argument over world history.

title: The Big-Gods Hypothesis
description: Watchful, moralising gods and cooperation among strangers: the theory, field games and island phylogenies

concepts.title: Watched People Are Nice People
concepts.contentHtml:
Some scholars argue that the gods and spirits of small hunter-gatherer societies are generally unconcerned with human morality, while the Big Gods familiar from major monotheistic and polytheistic traditions care intensely how you behave. In Big Gods: How Religion Transformed Cooperation and Conflict (2013), the psychologist Ara Norenzayan argued that the difference is no accident. Over the past ten thousand years, groups grew from bands into cities and empires full of strangers. Cooperation based on genetic relatedness, reciprocity and partner choice falters when transactions are fleeting and anonymous. Belief in increasingly knowing, punitive, moralising gods, Norenzayan proposed, helped fill the gap: watched people are nice people, and nice people drive social complexity.1

In its mature form, set out by Norenzayan and six co-authors in Behavioral and Brain Sciences, the theory is a hybrid. Religious beliefs first arose as non-adaptive by-products of ordinary cognition, as lessons 1 and 2 described.2 Then cultural evolution took over. A package of potent moralising gods, credible displays of faith and other bonding practices was selected because it promoted high fertility and cooperation with co-religionists, often helping groups win in competition and conflict. Successful groups expanded or were copied. Norenzayan has described his own shift: the by-product account is foundational, but it cannot do the job alone.

The idea of supernatural watchers has experimental support. In a 2011 study, children aged 5–6 and 8–9 attempted a hard rule-following task while told that an invisible person, Princess Alice, was watching, and were secretly filmed. Children's expressed belief in her significantly determined how long they held off cheating. When sceptical children were left out of the analysis, being told about Princess Alice inhibited cheating as effectively as a real adult in the room.3

The hypothesis therefore makes a sharp historical prediction: moralising gods should come before, and help cause, the growth of large societies. The rest of this lesson and the next two test it with field games, laboratory primes and world history.

concepts.title: Coins, Cups and a Die: Testing Gods in the Field
concepts.contentHtml:
To test Big Gods outside the laboratory, Benjamin Purzycki, Joseph Henrich, Norenzayan and colleagues took a single game to eight communities: inland and coastal Tanna in Vanuatu, Yasawa and Lovu in Fiji, Pesqueiro in Brazil, Pointe aux Piments in Mauritius, the Tyva Republic in Siberia and Hadzaland in Tanzania. The 591 participants followed traditions ranging from Christianity, Hinduism and Buddhism to animism and ancestor worship.

The Random Allocation Game is designed to catch quiet favouritism. A player sits with two cups, a stack of coins and a fair die with three sides of one colour and three of another.1 For each coin you choose a cup in your mind and roll: black sends the coin to the cup you chose, white to the other. The cups stand for real people, and nobody sees your choices, so you can cheat freely. With 30 rolls, honest play produces a binomial spread centred on 15 coins per cup, so bias shows up as a shifted distribution across the whole sample. In different versions one cup was the player's own or belonged to a local co-religionist, and the other belonged to an anonymous co-religionist living far away. The Hadza, the least market-integrated group, played for tokens worth 8 ounces of maize per roll.2

Overall, players favoured themselves and their local communities. But the more punitive and knowledgeable about human thoughts and actions people rated their moralistic gods, the more coins they gave to distant co-religionists relative to themselves and to local co-religionists.3 The 2016 Nature paper concluded that such beliefs can contribute to the expansion of prosociality.

Read the scope carefully. The effect concerned co-religionists, the measure was impartial rule-following rather than kindness to everyone, and the key result links individuals' beliefs to their choices. It shows an association in living people, not the historical order of events.

concepts.title: Phylogenies and Ecology: Which Came First?
concepts.contentHtml:
Cross-cultural surveys have long linked moralising high gods with complex societies. But treating each culture as an independent data point is a trap first noted by Francis Galton: cultures are related by descent and share traits through common ancestry, which can produce spurious correlations. A correlation also cannot say which trait came first.

In 2015 Joseph Watts, Russell Gray and colleagues used Austronesia as a natural laboratory. Its cultures range from the seminomadic band of the Palawan Batak to the complex state of Bali, and from localised ancestor worship to structured pantheons.1 Mapping traits for 96 Austronesian cultures onto language trees, they used Bayesian phylogenetic methods to infer the order in which traits evolved. They separated two hypotheses: moralising high gods (MHGs), and broad supernatural punishment, punishment by any of a wide range of moralising agents.

The result split the theory in two. Broad supernatural punishment appeared to drive political complexity, but MHGs followed it;2 the authors suggest the high-god concept diffused as part of a suite of traits exchanged between already complex societies. Their coding also excluded high gods clearly attributable to contact with Abrahamic religions. In Hawaii, the ancestors of chiefs were elevated to gods and gave chiefs authority and supernatural power, a reminder that supernatural punishment can serve political claims as well as cooperation.

Ecology adds another layer. A 2014 study by Botero and colleagues of 583 societies found belief in moralising high gods more prevalent among societies in poorer environments, more prone to ecological duress, and in politically complex societies that recognise rights to movable property.3 Their models predicted the global distribution with 91% accuracy and pointed to a mixture of social, cultural and environmental forces, neither pure cultural transmission nor simple ecological determinism.

title: Religious Priming and the Replication Record
description: God primes, generosity and analytic atheism: what survived large preregistered replications

concepts.title: God Is Watching You: the Original Primes
concepts.contentHtml:
If watched people are nice people, then merely reminding people of God should make them nicer. In 2007 Azim Shariff and Ara Norenzayan tested this with the dictator game, in which you divide money between yourself and an anonymous stranger who has no say. First, participants unscrambled sentences. For some, the words had religious meanings, a priming manipulation meant to activate God concepts implicitly. Primed participants gave more money to the anonymous stranger than those who saw neutral words or no prime,1 an effect at least as large as priming secular moral institutions. Self-reported religiosity, by contrast, did not seem to predict giving.

The authors weighed two mechanisms: an ideomotor effect, in which an activated concept nudges behaviour automatically, or a felt presence of supernatural watchers. Field work seemed to extend the result: Moroccan shopkeepers behaved more generously in an economic game during the Islamic call to prayer. Not every finding in this domain replicated, though; a 2017 study with a Japanese sample is cited as one that did not.

Priming became a workhorse because it promised causal experiments rather than correlations. In 2016 Shariff and colleagues meta-analysed 93 studies with 11,653 participants, combining effect-size analyses, p-curve analyses and adjustments for publication bias. They concluded that religious priming has robust effects across many outcome measures, prosocial ones included. There was one important twist. Priming did not reliably affect non-religious participants, suggesting that the effect depends on activating culturally transmitted religious beliefs rather than on some universal reflex.2

That twist matters for the big picture. A prime that works only on believers fits a cultural account of religion's social effects, but it also means that the lab effect is a measure of what belief does once acquired, not a demonstration of how belief arose.

concepts.title: Bias Corrections and Preregistered Replications
concepts.contentHtml:
A meta-analysis pools the published record, and the published record may be skewed towards positive results. In 2015 Michiel van Elk, Eric-Jan Wagenmakers and colleagues reanalysed the religious priming data with two bias-correcting methods. PET-PEESE, which regresses effect sizes on their precision to estimate what a perfectly precise study would find, suggested the effect was driven solely by publication bias.1 A Bayesian bias correction suggested a real effect remained. Two respectable methods gave opposite answers. The authors concluded that meta-analysis alone cannot settle a disputed effect, and called for a large-scale, preregistered replication project as the remedy for experimenter bias and publication bias.

Such replications were already arriving. In 2015 Gomes and McCullough repeated key elements of Shariff and Norenzayan's second experiment with 650 participants, adding a less conspicuous religious prime, a more explicit awareness probe and analyses suited to non-normal data. They found no statistically significant effect of religious priming.2 Their small meta-analysis of all known religious priming studies using the dictator game put the mean effect at no different from zero, and larger studies tended to report smaller effects, a pattern consistent with publication bias.

In 2018 Billingsley, Gomes and McCullough ran two further experiments online, where anonymity was virtually assured, one of them adding an option to take money. Religious participants transferred more on average than non-religious ones. But Bayesian analyses supported the null hypothesis that implicit religious priming did not increase transfers, even among religious subjects.3 Explicit priming had a small but reliable effect, again among religious subjects only. Their meta-analysis found the overall effect of implicit priming on dictator transfers small and not statistically different from zero.

The record therefore splits. Subtle, implicit God primes on generosity have not survived large replications; explicit reminders may nudge believers a little.

concepts.title: Analytic Atheism and The Thinker
concepts.contentHtml:
The same laboratory tradition produced a mirror-image claim. In Science in 2012, Will Gervais and Norenzayan reported that people more inclined to override flawed intuitions with analysis expressed more religious disbelief, and that four experiments using subtle triggers of analytic thinking also encouraged disbelief. In one, people who viewed images of Rodin's The Thinker reported lower belief in God than people who viewed Myron's Discobolus, with an effect size of d = −0.59 from groups of only 26 and 31.

In 2017 Clinton Sanchez, Robert Calin-Jageman and colleagues ran a precise, preregistered, multi-site replication of the Thinker study with 941 participants, drawn from a community college, a Catholic and a Lutheran university, and an online marketplace. The effect was d = 0.07, in the wrong direction.1 The original finding, they concluded, does not seem to provide reliable evidence that analytic thinking causes a decrease in religious belief. A 2017 set of three studies led by Miguel Farias, including a pilgrimage field study and a neurostimulation experiment, likewise found no relationship between intuitive or analytic thinking and supernatural belief.2

The correlational link has proved fickle too. In 2018 Gervais and colleagues tested 3,461 people in 13 diverse countries: analytic atheism appeared robustly only in aggregate analyses and in three individual countries.3 A 2025 preprint by Byrd, Stich and Sytsma, with more than 70,000 people from five of six continental regions and controls for confounds such as numeracy, did detect a small, reliable link. They traced it largely to analytic apostasy: better reflectors were likelier to have lost their childhood religion, and analytic atheism went undetected once apostates were excluded. Conversion was rare and unrelated to reflection.

The arc mirrors the wider replication crisis: striking small-sample experiments gave way to large samples, preregistration and smaller, more conditional claims.

title: Seshat: Big Gods on Trial in World History
description: The 2019 Nature paper, the missing-data critique, the 2021 retraction and the retake

concepts.title: A Databank of Ten Thousand Years
concepts.contentHtml:
Field games show associations in living people, but the Big Gods hypothesis is a claim about history. To test such claims at scale, the Seshat: Global History Databank codes the historical and archaeological record of past societies into variables that can be compared statistically. On 20 March 2019 Harvey Whitehouse, Pieter François, Patrick Savage, Peter Turchin and colleagues used it in a Nature paper titled “Complex societies precede moralizing gods throughout world history”.

The team coded records from 414 societies spanning the past 10,000 years in 30 regions, using 51 measures of social complexity and 4 measures of supernatural enforcement of morality.1 The analysis confirmed the association between moralising gods and social complexity but reversed the expected order: moralising gods followed, rather than preceded, large increases in social complexity. Powerful moralising big gods and prosocial supernatural punishment tended to appear only after the emergence of megasocieties with populations of more than around one million people.

The interpretation kept a role for religion. Moralising gods were not a prerequisite for social complexity, the authors argued, but they might help sustain and expand complex multi-ethnic empires once established. And rituals that standardise religious traditions across large populations, which they called doctrinal rituals, generally came before moralising gods. On this reading ritual practice mattered more than the content of belief for the initial rise of complexity, echoing Whitehouse's modes of religiosity from lesson 3.

Behind the headline sat a before-and-after comparison. For the 12 regions with complexity data both before and after the first evidence of moralising gods, the authors aligned each time series at that first appearance and compared complexity on either side.2 Everything therefore hinged on dating first appearances correctly, and on what counted as absence before them.

concepts.title: Missing Data Treated as Absence
concepts.contentHtml:
Seshat, like any historical database, is full of gaps. Bret Beheim and 14 co-authors inspected the data behind the 2019 paper. Several of them, including Norenzayan, Henrich, Gervais, Shariff, Willard and Slingerland, had co-authored the Behavioral and Brain Sciences synthesis of the Big Gods theory that the paper challenged. They found that 61% of the data points on moralising gods were missing values, mostly from smaller populations of under a million people, and that the analysis had re-coded these as known absences of moralising gods.1

Why does that matter? Imagine a region where the first well-attested moralising god belongs to a large state, while records about religion in the smaller societies before it are thin. If no information is converted into no moralising god, the first appearance is forced to coincide with the first good records, and the conclusion that gods follow complexity is partly built into the coding. When Beheim's team confined the analysis to the extant data, or used standard imputation methods for the missing values, the reported finding was reversed: moralising gods preceded increases in social complexity.2 They called the megasociety threshold an artefact of the decision to re-code missing data as absences. The critique appeared in Nature on 7 July 2021.

Historians raised a different worry. In a 2020 commentary in the Journal of Cognitive Historiography, Edward Slingerland and colleagues from the Database of Religious History voiced serious concerns about how the Seshat team had coded historical data,3 and about the lack of clarity over how involved expert historians had been. They warned that this approach risked permanently alienating academic historians, whom any large-scale project of this kind needs as collaborators.

Underneath lies an old philosophical question: when is absence of evidence evidence of absence? For a society known only from potsherds and a few inscriptions, the answer about its gods is rarely obvious.

concepts.title: Retraction, Retake and an Unsettled Question
concepts.contentHtml:
On 7 July 2021, alongside the critique, Nature published a retraction note. The authors accepted that in portions of their dataset before the dates of first appearance they should have labelled moralising gods as absent or inferred absent, rather than converting unknowns to zeros during analysis.1 They maintained that refined analyses still strongly supported their conclusions, but judged the differences substantial enough to warrant retraction. Three authors, John Baines, Alan Covey and Kevin Feeney, did not agree with the retraction.2

The corrected and extended version appeared in 2022 as a retake in Religion, Brain & Behavior. It reanalysed an expanded Seshat database with a revised codebook, improved data management and a more direct statistical test of causal order. It reported that correcting the missing-data errors did not significantly change the main finding:3 the largest increases in social complexity preceded Big Gods, which did not contribute to sociopolitical complexity as the hypothesis predicted. Replying to commentators, Turchin, Whitehouse and colleagues argued that warfare intensity and agricultural productivity drove both social complexity and moralising religion, so the two correlate through shared causes rather than one causing the other.4 They also rejected the charge that their inferred-absent codings lacked a basis in the record, pointing to 210 pages of analytical narratives and 219 pages of tables.

So where does that leave you? The SEP's 2026 survey reports a field still divided over whether big gods or big societies came first.5 Whether the error was a mislabelling of still-valuable data or a fundamental flaw depends on which team you ask, and on wider assumptions about statistical inference and about using databank codes to test history. The Austronesian phylogenies, the field games and the Seshat analyses each answer a slightly different question, so they can be partly right at once.

title: Does Explaining Belief Debunk It?
description: Evolutionary debunking arguments, the main replies, and what CSR means for believers and sceptics

concepts.title: The Shape of a Debunking Argument
concepts.contentHtml:
Suppose CSR is broadly right: agency detection, mind-reading, teleology, memorable concepts, ritual and cultural selection together explain why most humans have believed in gods. Does that undercut the belief? Philosophers broadly agree on two starting points. First, uncovering the origins of a belief does not by itself show that it is false;1 inferring falsity from origins alone is the genetic fallacy. Second, under the right circumstances, learning how a belief arose can still pose an epistemic problem for it.

Jason Marsh's SEP entry illustrates the difference with two music fans. Sara believes Taylor Swift likes her because a highly unreliable tabloid said so; once she learns this, holding on looks irrational. Anahita believes she is watching Taylor Swift on stage because she is at the concert and can see her; learning how human vision evolved changes nothing. The question is which case the believer resembles.

The standard debunking argument, imported from debates about evolution and morality, has two premises. The causal premise says the belief is explained by some process. The epistemic premise says that process is off-track, not responsive to the truth. The conclusion is that the belief is unjustified. Applied to religion, the simplest version notes that HADD is a better-safe-than-sorry mechanism that produces many false positives, so beliefs it generates about unseen agents are unreliable.

That version is too quick. Even if HADD were foundational, and lesson 2 showed that it is contested, it would not give a complete account of belief. Stronger versions widen the causal premise to the whole CSR toolkit and to cultural selection, asking whether believing in order to belong or to cooperate is likely to track religious truth. Matthew Braddock's debunking argument from false beliefs adds that, given their diverse outputs, CSR-style explanations support suspending judgement about the whole class of god beliefs.2

concepts.title: Replies: Naive Epistemology and Independent Reasons
concepts.contentHtml:
Theists and many neutral epistemologists push back along several lines.

  • The metaphysical reply. If God exists necessarily, asking what people would believe were there no God is confused; Michael Murray remarked that he does not think there would be a universe at all if there were no God. Critics answer that the challenge is epistemic, and epistemic possibilities can revise one's metaphysics.
  • Naive epistemology. The epistemic premise often relies on sensitivity: if p were false, you would not believe p. Most contemporary epistemologists reject sensitivity as a requirement for knowledge because of its sweeping sceptical implications.1 If we were brains in vats we would still believe in a physical world; should we all become external-world sceptics? Since every faculty has natural origins, debunking arguments risk overgeneralising, perhaps even to mathematics.
  • Independent reasons. Some believers have grounds that CSR does not touch: natural theology, testimony, or religious experience, a route Kelly James Clark and Justin Barrett have explored.2 If you really did hear Taylor Swift say she likes you, past gullibility about tabloids would not spoil that belief.

Each reply has critics. Helen De Cruz and Johan De Smedt question whether natural theological arguments are really independent of the intuitions CSR describes. Joshua Thurow, who denies that debunking arguments fully undermine belief, concedes that if CSR predicts rationalisation in how beliefs are maintained, awareness of that could produce partial defeat and call for less confidence. Lari Launonen allows that some ordinary religious experiences may be undercut. A bolder Moorean move, modelled on Thomas Nagel's stance on moral realism, simply reverses the inference: the belief is true, so the debunking story must be false. Many find that unjustifiably dogmatic, including religious academics who want to accommodate evolutionary science.

The emerging middle view is that the truth lies somewhere between full defeat and no problem at all, and that debunking arguments will not go away soon.

concepts.title: Beyond Debunking: For, Against or Neutral?
concepts.contentHtml:
CSR can cut more than one way. Some philosophers revive the consensus gentium, or common consent, argument: if belief in the divine is rooted in our shared human constitution, its prevalence might count as a broad natural sign of the divine. Others draw the opposite moral. Alvin Goldman builds a Bayesian challenge to common-consent arguments. Jason and Jon Marsh pose an explanatory challenge of religious diversity: if God cares about the details of belief, why design minds and environments in which so many competing traditions naturally arise?1 A related problem of natural nonbelief argues that the absence of theistic concepts among early humans favours naturalism over theism.

Then there is coexistence reasoning. Boyer describes a community that explains a collapsed mud-house roof both by termites and by witchcraft, and people across cultures, including in medical settings, combine natural and supernatural explanations. Peter van Inwagen thinks CSR can be given a providential reading, but offers a limiting case: a weeping statue of the Virgin turns out to be weeping bat urine. A supernatural story remains logically possible, yet clinging to the miracle would be contrived. Is CSR more like the bat urine, or like a natural process God could have planned?

Finally, is the field atheistic by design? Some rhetoric suggests so. Jesse Bering was reported in 2006 as saying that “We've got God by the throat and I'm not going to stop until one of us is dead.” Yet Justin Barrett, a theist, is a prominent contributor who builds the field's findings into his faith,2 and Daniel Dennett said the spell he wanted to break was the idea that religion cannot be studied scientifically. For most researchers CSR is a descriptive, bottom-up science, and its wider implications are a separate philosophical question that believers and sceptics can argue on equal terms.
